A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VICtoR and provide readable text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices. Their corresponding methods and experiments can be matched despite reorganization and revised displays.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulated policy-learning results, reward-component ablations, XSkill reward visualizations, and task-knowledge generation accuracy.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds contrastive-loss ablations, automatic annotation agreement measurements, and computational-cost measurements.

M1.justification: The task knowledge generator, stage detector, motion progress evaluator, losses, inference rules, and reward formulation remain unchanged. The newly described classifier architecture is additional implementation detail. The GPT-4V annotation study does not establish a change to VICtoR's training or inference pipeline.

E1.justification: The simulated manipulation environment and XSkill task and object coverage are retained. The new annotation analysis examines object-state labeling within existing XSkill coverage. v2 Table 12 documents tasks already visualized in v1 Figures 9–10; the demonstration-count revision changes sample quantity rather than coverage.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain Sparse Reward, Stage Reward, LIV, LOReL, and VICtoR(task), with unchanged comparator membership in Tables 1–2 and the matched visualizations. Newly discussed motion-decomposition methods are not evaluated as baselines.

E3.justification: v1 Appendix B.1 reports 100 demonstrations per VICtoR motion and per baseline task; v2 Appendix C.1 reports 150 for both. This is a reported training-budget revision, without evidence establishing reruns. Added studies introduce loss-removal controls, GPT-4V label-agreement evaluation using MDETR crops, and timing measurements over 1,000 steps.

E4.justification: v2 adds separate tests of all three contrastive losses in Appendix B.3 and an automatic object-state annotation feasibility and error analysis in B.4. These substantially expand analysis beyond v1's reward-level ablation and task-knowledge accuracy test. The existing task-complexity analysis moves into Section 5.4 with revised VICtoR traces, while misordered-action analysis remains.

E5.justification: Both versions report three-seed averages for Tables 1–3 and standard-deviation shading in the policy-learning curves. The added loss and annotation studies do not introduce seed counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or other uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 retain identical numerical results. New Table 4 reports 0.0%, 61.8%, and 94.0% success when removing the language-frame, motion, and time contrastive losses respectively, versus 96.4% with all losses. Figure 9 adds annotation agreement of 96.88% for cloth, 94.87% for light, 90.63% for oven, and 88.10% for drawer. VICtoR potential traces are revised, and runtime measurements are added; these do not establish a same-setting performance improvement over v1.

T1.justification: The POMDP formulation, mathematical definitions, and Equations 1–9 remain unchanged. The new contrastive-loss illustration explains existing objectives without adding formal reasoning, assumptions, or proofs.

C1.justification: The central hierarchical reward-model and motion-only training claims remain. However, the introduction changes the subgroup associated with the 43% advantage from the top half of tasks by motion count to tasks with more than four motions. This narrows the stated claim inconsistently with Section 5.2 and Tables 1–2, which support the more-than-three-motion grouping.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the loss ablation as supporting each objective, especially language-frame contrast. It also attributes annotation disagreements mainly to ambiguous motion transitions, argues that automatic labeling makes deployment feasible, and discusses inference latency as practically acceptable. The limitation concerning unseen motions is unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 specifies the stage classifier's CLIP encoders and downstream MLP, documents 120 XSkill demonstrations split into three motion-level videos each, and adds motion descriptions in Table 12. Appendix C.5 adds training costs, inference timings, and associated hardware. Existing hyperparameter tables, software details, and task-generation prompts are largely retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds Chain-of-Thought Predictive Control and Universal Visual Decomposer to the references. Appendix E adds a focused comparison distinguishing VICtoR's stage-motion-progress reward hierarchy from prior motion decomposition for imitation learning.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction receive localized rewriting, an existing qualitative analysis becomes Section 5.4, and appendix subsections are reorganized. Acknowledgements and publication-header changes are added. Most method prose, conclusions, limitations, and prompt content remain unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 combines an ICLR-format layout revision with new loss illustrations and annotation visualizations in Figures 7 and 9, and new Tables 4 and 12. v1 Figure 6 moves into the main text as Figure 4 with revised VICtoR traces and axes. Appendix tables are regrouped, while the original learning-curve and XSkill visualization panels are retained.

improvement.justification: The added loss ablations provide previously missing evidence about the training objectives, while classifier, XSkill, and runtime details improve reproducibility and practical assessment. These focused gains outweigh the new inconsistency in the introduction's 43% task subgroup. The annotation study supports labeling feasibility but does not validate downstream policy performance using automatic labels, limiting the overall improvement.
